cards.explanation: The answer is to pay whatever he demands. Hezekiah, Judah's king, says, “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me.” That's a blank check, friends. It's like telling a stranger "name your number" and then holding your breath. Sennacherib, Assyria's king, names it in the very next line.

The answer is the LORD's house and the palace treasuries. Hezekiah hands over all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. That's two places he's pulling silver from. It's like checking every coat pocket and couch cushion you own for change. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is trying to cover what Assyria demanded.

The answer is gold. Hezekiah stripped the gold he had plated on the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD. Think about that, friends. It's like peeling the shine right off your own front door to cover a bill. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is giving up what he had put there himself.

The answer is False, and that's the sting of it. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army…” Hezekiah, Judah's king, had already sent his payment. Think of sending a payment and still having a collector show up at your door.

The answer is False. Hezekiah doesn't go out. The Assyrians called for the king, and Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder went out to them. So the army asks for the king and gets his staff. That's like asking to see the manager and getting three people from the front desk.

The answer is what it is based on. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “What is the basis of this confidence of yours?” Basis means what it's standing on. Hezekiah's confidence is under the microscope, and the Rabshakeh wants to see the foundation. He opens with a question, and a pointed one.

The answer is Egypt. The Rabshakeh says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it.” He also names Pharaoh king of Egypt. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, has his claim ready, and it comes with a picture.

The answer is True. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem: ‘You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?” That's his answer ready for anyone who says they trust the LORD. He's bringing up what Hezekiah did and quoting him back.

The answer is that Judah has to find riders for them. Here's the catch: “…if you can put riders on them!” Two thousand horses sounds generous until you see the fine print, friends. It's like being given a free car when you don't have a driver. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, is poking at Judah with this one.

The answer is the LORD. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’…” That's what he claims. It's the boldest thing he's said so far.

The answer is that they ask him to speak to them in Aramaic. They say, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak with us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.” Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder are the three speaking. I think they wanted this talk kept from the people listening, but the text only gives us the request itself. It's a request about language.

The answer is False. The request is turned down. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, answers, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…” He says the men on the wall are meant to hear it too. Asking him to keep it quiet didn't work.

The answer is that he calls out loudly in Hebrew. The Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. Hebrew is the very language the three officials had asked him not to use in the hearing of the people on the wall. Now he's using it at full volume.

The answer is False. He says Hezekiah can't. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, tells the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand.” He's speaking right to the people on the wall. He wants them doubting their own king.

The answer is True. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’” He's quoting what Hezekiah says and telling the people not to be persuaded by it. That's his line, and he's repeating it to the whole wall.

The answer is that he will take them to a land like their own. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, speaks of the vine, the fig tree and the cistern, then says, “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” So the picture he paints has a move in it. It's a sales pitch with a move hidden inside.

The answer is Samaria. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” It's a roll call, and Samaria is the last name on it. He's counting off places like a man reading a very long guest list.

The answer is True. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, finishes with, “Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” He lines up all those place names and then points his question straight at Jerusalem. It's the end of his big speech.

The answer is that they stay completely silent. The text says, “But the people remained silent and did not answer a word…” After all that shouting, nobody says a thing. I'd have at least cleared my throat, friends.

The answer is True. The text gives the reason. The people “…remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded…” them not to answer him. So their quiet wasn't an accident. Hezekiah, Judah's king, gave an order, and the wall followed it.

The answer is that their clothes are torn. They came to Hezekiah “…with their clothes torn…” That's Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, the same three who went out to the Rabshakeh. The text doesn't say why their clothes were torn. I think the words they heard hit them hard.
